title: Case Study: Splitwise
summary: Design an expense-sharing app end to end — split strategies, a balance-tracking data model, and the greedy algorithm that simplifies debts.

blocks.markdown: **Design Splitwise**: an app where users form groups, log shared expenses paid by one or more people, split the cost by different rules, and always know who owes whom — down to a minimal set of settling payments.

blocks.subTitle: Why this problem
blocks.markdown:
It's a favorite LLD interview because the hard part isn't CRUD — it's the **money-splitting logic** and keeping a **balance map** correct as expenses pile up.

- Tests **Strategy** (split types) and **Factory** (building the right split) together — see [creational-patterns](creational-patterns) and [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i).
- Use [lld-interview-framework](lld-interview-framework) as the general approach; this topic applies it end to end.

blocks.subTitle: Functional
blocks.markdown:
What the system must do:

- **Users & groups** — users can form a group (trip, flat, team) to share ongoing expenses.
- **Add an expense** paid by one user, or **split across multiple payers**.
- **Split types**: EQUAL, EXACT (fixed amounts), PERCENT (percentage shares).
- **Track balances** — who owes whom, and how much, at any time.
- **Settle up** — record a payment that clears (part of) a debt.
- **Simplify debts** — collapse a tangle of IOUs into the fewest payments.

blocks.subTitle: Non-functional
blocks.markdown:
What the system must guarantee, not just do:

- **Correctness** — the sum of all balances must always net to zero; money can't appear or vanish.
- **Consistency under concurrency** — two expenses added at once must both land in the balance sheet, not overwrite each other.
- **Extensibility** — a new split type should plug in without touching `Expense` or `BalanceSheet`.

Correctness is the one non-functional requirement that shapes the data model directly — see the Balance data model card.

**Noun extraction**: underline the nouns in the requirements and each becomes a candidate class.

| Noun in requirements | Becomes |
|---|---|
| user, group | `User`, `Group` |
| expense, split | `Expense`, `Split` hierarchy |
| balance, payment | `BalanceSheet`, `Settlement` |

The verb "split the cost" isn't a field — it's a **policy** that varies by type, so it becomes a **Strategy** (`Split`), not an `if/else` inside `Expense`.

- **Composition**: a group owns its expenses; an expense owns its splits.
- The `Split` hierarchy sits behind a **Strategy** interface so `Expense` never branches on split type.

blocks.subTitle: User & Group
blocks.markdown:
A group is just a named set of users plus the expenses logged against it.

```text
class User:
    id: String
    name: String
    email: String

class Group:
    id: String
    name: String
    members: List<User>
    expenses: List<Expense>

    method addMember(user: User):
        members.add(user)

    method addExpense(expense: Expense, balanceSheet: BalanceSheet):
        expenses.add(expense)
        balanceSheet.apply(expense)   // see BalanceSheet card
```

blocks.subTitle: Split hierarchy — Strategy
blocks.markdown:
"How much does each person owe?" is a policy that varies by type — that variation is the textbook case for **Strategy**.

```text
abstract class Split:
    user: User
    amount: Money      // filled in by validate(), the owed share

    abstract method validate(totalAmount: Money, splits: List<Split>): boolean

class EqualSplit extends Split:
    method validate(totalAmount, splits): boolean:
        share = totalAmount / splits.size()
        for s in splits: s.amount = share
        return true

class ExactSplit extends Split:
    // amount is set directly by the caller
    method validate(totalAmount, splits): boolean:
        sum = splits.sumOf(s -> s.amount)
        return sum == totalAmount

class PercentSplit extends Split:
    percent: float

    method validate(totalAmount, splits): boolean:
        if splits.sumOf(s -> s.percent) != 100:
            return false
        for s in splits: s.amount = totalAmount * (s.percent / 100)
        return true
```

blocks.subTitle: SplitFactory
blocks.markdown:
Building the right `Split` subclass from a type string is a **Factory** — callers never say `new PercentSplit()` directly.

```text
enum SplitType:
    EQUAL
    EXACT
    PERCENT

class SplitFactory:
    static method create(type: SplitType, user: User, value: float): Split:
        switch type:
            case EQUAL:   return new EqualSplit(user)
            case EXACT:   return new ExactSplit(user, amount = value)
            case PERCENT: return new PercentSplit(user, percent = value)
```

blocks.subTitle: Expense
blocks.markdown:
An expense supports **multiple payers** — not just one — which is why `paidBy` is a map, not a single user.

```text
class Expense:
    id: String
    description: String
    amount: Money
    paidBy: Map<User, Money>     // supports split payment, not just one payer
    splits: List<Split>
    splitType: SplitType

    constructor(description, amount, paidBy, splitType, splits):
        this.description = description
        this.amount = amount
        this.paidBy = paidBy
        this.splitType = splitType
        this.splits = splits
        if not splitType.validate(amount, splits):   // delegates to Strategy
            throw InvalidSplitException()
        if paidBy.values().sum() != amount:
            throw InvalidPaymentException()
```

The **balance sheet** is a nested map: `Map<User, Map<User, Amount>>` — `balances[A][B]` reads as "A owes B this much."

- Only one direction is stored per pair at a time; a positive `balances[A][B]` and `balances[B][A]` are netted so they don't both exist.
- This shape answers "who owes whom" in **O(1)** per pair, and "total owed by A" in one row scan — no need to replay every expense.

blocks.subTitle: BalanceSheet — updating on each expense
Settling up
blocks.markdown:
A settlement is just a debt-reducing entry into the same map — it doesn't need its own storage structure.

```text
class SettlementService:
    method settle(sheet: BalanceSheet, payer: User, payee: User, amount: Money):
        owed = sheet.getBalance(payer, payee)
        if amount > owed:
            throw OverpaymentException()
        sheet.adjust(payer, payee, -amount)   // reduces payer's debt to payee
```

The three split types differ only in how they compute `amount` per user — the rest of `Expense` treats them identically.

| Split type | Input required | Validation rule |
|---|---|---|
| EQUAL | just the user list | `total / count`, no input to check |
| EXACT | amount per user | sum of amounts == total |
| PERCENT | percent per user | percentages sum to 100 |

All three implement the same `Split` interface, so `Expense` calls `validate()` polymorphically without knowing which one it got.

blocks.subTitle: The problem
blocks.markdown:
After many expenses, the balance sheet can have A owing B, B owing C, and C owing A — a cycle of debts that nets to fewer actual payments than it looks like.

**Debt simplification** replaces the tangle with the **minimum number of transactions** that settle the same net amounts — pure bookkeeping cleanup, it changes no one's total owed or owing.

blocks.subTitle: Greedy algorithm
blocks.markdown:
Reduce every user to one **net** number (positive = owed money, negative = owes money), then greedily match the biggest creditor with the biggest debtor.

```text
method simplifyDebts(sheet: BalanceSheet, users: List<User>): List<Settlement>:
    net: Map<User, Money> = {}
    for u in users:
        net[u] = sum over v of (sheet.getBalance(v, u) - sheet.getBalance(u, v))

    creditors = maxHeap of users where net[u] > 0, keyed by net[u]
    debtors   = maxHeap of users where net[u] < 0, keyed by -net[u]
    result: List<Settlement> = []

    while creditors.notEmpty() and debtors.notEmpty():
        creditor = creditors.peekMax()
        debtor = debtors.peekMax()
        amount = min(net[creditor], -net[debtor])

        result.add(new Settlement(debtor, creditor, amount))
        net[creditor] -= amount
        net[debtor] += amount

        if net[creditor] == 0: creditors.popMax()
        if net[debtor] == 0: debtors.popMax()

    return result
```

Where each pattern earns its place in this design:

| Pattern | Where it's used |
|---|---|
| Strategy | `Split` hierarchy — EQUAL/EXACT/PERCENT vary independently |
| Factory | `SplitFactory` builds the right `Split` from a type + value |
| Observer (optional) | notify group members when a new expense or settlement posts |

Each replaces an `if/else` chain that would otherwise sit inside `Expense`. See [creational-patterns](creational-patterns) and [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i) for the general form.

blocks.subTitle: Balances drifting from zero
blocks.markdown:
**The classic bug**: rounding a PERCENT or EQUAL split (e.g. splitting ₹100 three ways → 33.33 each) leaves a stray cent, and over thousands of expenses the sheet slowly stops summing to zero.

- Fix: after distributing rounded shares, add the **leftover remainder** to one designated split (usually the payer's own share) so the total always reconciles exactly.
- Never trust a running total — periodically assert that `sum(all balances[A][B] - balances[B][A])` across every pair equals zero; a nonzero sum means a bug already shipped.

blocks.subTitle: Modeling split types
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you model EQUAL, EXACT, and PERCENT splits?**

A `Split` interface (or abstract class) with one method, `validate(totalAmount, splits)`, implemented by `EqualSplit`, `ExactSplit`, and `PercentSplit` — classic **Strategy**. `Expense` calls `validate()` once and never branches on type. A `SplitFactory` builds the right subclass from a `SplitType` enum so callers don't `new` concrete classes directly.

blocks.subTitle: Tracking who owes whom
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you track balances — who owes whom?**

A nested map, `Map<User, Map<User, Amount>>`, where `balances[A][B]` means "A owes B this much." Every new expense calls `BalanceSheet.apply()` once to adjust the map incrementally — balances are never recomputed by replaying the full expense history, which keeps every lookup O(1) per pair.

blocks.subTitle: How debt simplification works
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How does debt simplification work?**

Collapse each user to one net number (total owed minus total owing). Push positive-net users into a max-heap of creditors and negative-net users into a max-heap of debtors, then greedily settle the biggest creditor against the biggest debtor, repeating until both heaps drain. This greedy match is optimal for minimizing transaction *count* in the common case and runs in O(n log n).

blocks.subTitle: Which patterns fit
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Which design patterns fit Splitwise, and why?**

Strategy for `Split` — the split rule changes independently of `Expense` and of the other split types. Factory for `SplitFactory` — it hides which concrete `Split` subclass gets built from a type flag. Observer is a natural add-on if the app needs to push notifications when an expense or settlement is posted, though it's not required for correctness.

blocks.subTitle: Keeping balances consistent
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do you keep balances consistent as expenses and settlements pile up?**

Route every mutation — new expense or settlement — through the single `BalanceSheet.apply()`/`adjust()` path, never a shortcut that writes the map directly. Wrap each adjustment in a transaction (or lock per user pair) so concurrent expense adds can't interleave and corrupt a cell. Periodically assert the sheet nets to zero across all pairs to catch drift from rounding early, as covered in the pitfall card.
